title: Dedicated performance profiles: customer-facing expectations, what we disclose, and SLA implications
creator: Lauren Bishop
project: Hardware tuning profiles pack (Serving Runtime Performance — Kernel + Scheduling)
description:
Context
- Runtime team is landing a versioned “hardware tuning profiles pack” (H100/L40S now; B200 preview) to make serving performance more predictable and observable.
- Dedicated customers are sensitive to changes in tail latency and throughput; they also expect clear guidance on what is “stable” vs “tunable” and what will/ won’t change during upgrades.
- This PM spec defines:
  1) What expectations we set for performance consistency on Dedicated
  2) What we surface to customers (docs + console), and what we keep internal
  3) How profile versioning/pinning interacts with Dedicated SLOs/SLAs, comms, and support processes

Goals
- Provide a consistent, supportable story to customers: performance is *profiled* per hardware SKU + workload shape; changes are versioned, observable, and (for Dedicated) controllable via pin/rollback.
- Reduce escalations caused by “silent” tuning changes by aligning on what we expose, when we notify, and how to troubleshoot.
- Ensure SLA language is not inadvertently expanded by publishing overly specific low-level tuning details.

Non-goals
- This is not a public marketing page; this is customer-facing enablement for Dedicated (sales/CS/support + customers who request it).
- We are not committing to fixed tokens/sec numbers in SLA. We will provide ranges / “expected behavior” guidance and a reproducible benchmarking method upon request.

Customer expectations to set (Dedicated)
1) Consistency
- Within a Dedicated deployment pinned to a given profile version and runtime version, performance should be stable within expected variance (region/hardware topology dependent).
- Across regions: we target comparable performance for the same SKU class, but variance can occur due to fleet differences (driver/CUDA, PCIe vs SXM, etc.). We will document known differences and provide compatibility checks.

2) Change control
- Default profile changes are treated as a “performance-affecting change.”
- Dedicated customers can:
  - Pin a profile_version (and optionally a profile_id) for change control
  - Roll back to a prior profile_version if regressions are observed
- Redwood may introduce new profile versions that improve perf/cost/reliability; we will not force-switch pinned customers without an agreed change window.

3) What we will measure with them (shared vocabulary)
- Latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) for prefill and decode (where available)
- Throughput (tokens/sec), error rates, and queueing time under load
- OOM / admission-control rejections (if any) and kernel fallback rate (as an indicator of “not using the fast path”)

4) Guardrails and “why you might see changes”
- Customers may see performance changes when:
  - They upgrade runtime versions
  - They change model versions/quantization
  - Their traffic shape shifts across workload buckets (prompt length, concurrency)
  - Fleet maintenance changes driver/CUDA within a supported window

What we will surface to customers
A) Console / operational visibility (minimum viable)
- Show in Dedicated debugging views:
  - active profile_id (e.g., h100-default-latency-v1)
  - active profile_version (e.g., 1.0.3)
  - detected sku (H100/L40S/B200) and compatibility status (supported/unsupported/warn)
- Show “last change” record for profile (timestamp + actor if customer-initiated; or Redwood change window if Redwood-initiated)
- Do NOT surface raw knob-level configuration by default (can be available to support under controlled sharing)

B) Customer docs / enablement materials
- “Performance profiles by hardware (Dedicated)” doc including:
  - A plain-English explanation of profiles and what they control
  - Expected behavior tables per SKU (qualitative + directional):
    - best for (latency vs throughput)
    - known constraints (memory headroom, concurrency caps)
    - common failure modes (e.g., L40S OOM under burst)
  - How to pin/rollback (step-by-step + who to contact)
  - What data to provide in a perf ticket: profile_version, runtime version, model, traffic shape, region

C) Release notes expectations
- Runtime release notes must mention:
  - if default profile_version changes
  - if scheduler/batching defaults change materially
  - any known regressions and mitigations (including recommended pin)

What we will NOT surface (by default)
- Exact kernel names/variants, kernel selection rules, or internal counters that could be misinterpreted as SLAs (“v3 attention kernel always used”).
- Exact concurrency limits / queue depths as contractual guarantees; instead we describe “recommended operating envelope” and note that admission control may engage to prevent instability.
- Fleet-internal instance type mappings or hardware topology details beyond SKU class, unless needed for a specific incident.

SLO / SLA alignment (Dedicated)
- Dedicated SLA remains uptime + API correctness + agreed latency SLOs where contracted.
- Profiles are a mechanism to *meet* SLOs more reliably; they are not a new SLA dimension.
- Customer-facing language proposal:
  - “Redwood provides hardware-specific performance profiles that are versioned and can be pinned for change control. Redwood may recommend profile updates to improve latency/throughput or reliability; customers may adopt these updates during a scheduled change window.”

Change management policy (Dedicated)
- Default behavior for Dedicated:
  - Existing Dedicated deployments: remain on current pinned profile_version unless customer opts into auto-updates.
  - New Dedicated deployments: default to latest stable profile_version for the SKU.
- Opt-in modes:
  1) “Pinned” (default for enterprise): no automatic profile_version changes
  2) “Recommended updates”: Redwood can auto-advance profile_version within a major version line, with email notice and rollback option
- Rollback semantics:
  - Rollback = change profile_version (and optionally revert runtime if required). Rollback should be auditable.

Support / escalation playbook (customer-facing expectations)
- When customer reports perf regression:
  1) Confirm profile_version + runtime version + model + region
  2) Compare to expected behavior for SKU + traffic bucket
  3) If regression aligns with a recent profile change, propose pin/rollback as immediate mitigation
  4) Collect benchmark traces or run a scoped benchmark-lab reproduction (internal)

Open questions (need alignment)
1) Do we allow customers to pin profile_id in addition to profile_version, or only version? (My proposal: allow both, but UI defaults to version.)
2) What is the customer-visible naming scheme for profile_id (human-readable vs opaque)?
3) For “Recommended updates” mode, what is the minimum notice period? (Proposal: 3 business days for non-emergency; immediate for security/stability hotfix with post-hoc notice.)
4) Do we provide any “expected tokens/sec range” in dedicated docs? (Proposal: only in private enablement decks / deal-room, not in docs, unless explicitly caveated.)

Acceptance criteria
- Dedicated customer-facing doc draft completed and reviewed by Runtime + SRE + Support enablement.
- Agreed console fields: profile_id + profile_version + sku + compatibility status.
- Agreed language for Dedicated MSA/SLA addendum guidance (at minimum internal legal-facing blurb; no contract change required for runtime-1.22).
- Clear support guidance on pin/rollback and what to collect during perf escalations.

comments: 2026-01-22 (Lauren Bishop): Drafted initial positioning: profiles as a change-control mechanism for Dedicated, not a new SLA dimension. Need Runtime to confirm what’s realistically observable in Console for 1.22.

2026-01-29 (Sean Gallagher): +1 to pin/rollback narrative. Please be explicit that admission control may reject requests under overload to protect tail latency; we should not promise “always accept” at any concurrency.

2026-02-02 (Irene Choi): Caution on cross-region equivalence claims. We can say “same SKU class,” but driver/CUDA spread and PCIe vs SXM can materially affect p99. Recommend we expose a compatibility status and keep instance-type mapping internal.

2026-02-07 (Mateo Alvarez): Agree we should not publish kernel variant names. We can expose profile_id/version + sku + a few high-level mode labels (latency-optimized vs throughput-optimized). Anything deeper should stay support-only.

2026-02-12 (Elliot Price): For docs: suggest we mirror the internal “expected behavior” tables but remove exact knob values and replace with plain-language ranges + symptoms/mitigations. Please provide a list of must-have tables per SKU.

2026-02-18 (Lauren Bishop): Marking In Review. Incorporated SRE/Infra feedback; remaining open question is notice period + whether we expose profile_id in customer UI or only version. Syncing with DES-214 owner before final.
